results.question: What does the book say about making your own chroma keyer?
results.answer:
The book's answer is: **you can build a basic chroma keyer yourself, but the author doesn't think it's worth it** — unlike the DIY luma key, where cleverness can beat the basic built-in tools, an off-the-shelf chroma keyer is "hard to improve upon" [S2].

**What a chroma keyer is.** The book defines chroma-keying as a keying technique that separates an object from its background based on colors unique to either the foreground or background [S11], specifically by creating a matte from a thresholded color [S20]. Internally, a chroma keyer converts the RGB image to HSV/HSL (because saturation is not an RGB attribute), sets a starting pixel value as the "center" of the key, and defines separate ranges for Hue, Saturation, and Value — pixels inside the ranges go to 100% white, outside go to black, with tolerances added for soft edges [S14][S3]. The author also flags a terminology wrinkle: many tools called "chroma keyers" (Keylight, Ultimatte) are really color-difference keyers; only Primatte is a true, sophisticated 3D chroma keyer [S4].

**The DIY method.** Section 2.2.2 recaps the recipe [S1][S17]:

1. Start with an operation that converts the RGB image to HSV.
2. Pipe the HSV image into a color curve node.
3. Keep track of the channel mapping: the **RED** curve now holds Hue, the **GREEN** curve holds Saturation, and the **BLUE** curve holds Value (brightness).
4. Adjust the three curves to include or exclude the Hue, Saturation, and Value ranges of the target object.

**A fancier variation.** The book also describes a three-dimensional color keyer based on grossly simplified Primatte principles: instead of working in HSV, you plot the green backing pixels in the RGB color cube and key on any arbitrary color [S8]. The formula given is a distance calculation — take the normalized RGB value of your center color (R1G1B1, the color you want to isolate) and of each pixel (R2G2B2) — which you can enter into a math node or equivalent expression to build your own 3D keyer [S13]. Test images are supplied: `WWW Chroma key target.tif` for practicing chroma and luma keys [S5] and `greenscreen.tiff` for the 3D version [S13].

**Practical verdict.** The section closes on a cautionary note: "making your own chroma keyer will probably be more hassle than it's worth — you might try it once to test your mettle, but an off-the-shelf chroma keyer is hard to improve upon" [S2]. This sits alongside the book's broader warning that pulling any key, even from a perfect greenscreen, is fundamentally flawed mathematics that merely works well under most circumstances [S18], and that chroma keys carry their own list of limitations and liabilities (explored later in the chapter) [S15]. So: useful as a learning exercise for understanding hue/saturation/luminance channels, but not as a production tool.

results.question: What does the book say about nonsquare pixels?
results.answer:
**The book defines a nonsquare pixel as one whose width and height are unequal — the width-to-height ratio is called the *pixel aspect ratio* (PAR), and this is independent of the image's overall aspect ratio [S1][S3][S10].** On an ordinary, properly adjusted computer monitor every pixel is square, so its PAR is 1:1 [S1]. Nonsquare (rectangular) pixels arise when a system's *display* aspect ratio differs from the aspect ratio of the underlying digital image [S2].

**Where nonsquare pixels come from (film and video).** Systems that "temporarily unsqueeze" an image are said to display nonsquare pixels — but the physical pixels on your monitor stay properly proportioned; only the display is geometrically transformed, and the underlying image data is never modified [S4]. In film, the same idea appears as optically distorted **squeezed** or **anamorphic** formats, like Cinemascope's 2:1 squeeze [S7][S5]. In video, standard-definition formats use rectangular pixels (NTSC-DV is 720 × 480, PAL-DV 720 × 576), whereas HD, graphics software, and computer monitors all use square pixels [S8].

**Why it matters in production and post.** The classic trap: if you create a digitally perfect circle and send it straight to NTSC video — whose pixel aspect ratio is 10:11, making pixels slightly taller than wide — the circle displays as an ellipse, stretched 11/10ths vertically; you may need to scale the image manually before output, unless your system automates it [S13]. Rotation is another pitfall: a small rotation applied to an element while still squeezed (e.g., 5°) produces a subtle but visible distortion, so the correct workflow is to **unsqueeze, rotate, then resqueeze along the x-axis** [S9]. The book's bottom line: if you work with nonsquare pixels, double-check everything so these problems don't slip into the final result [S9].

results.question: What does the book say about oebps/ritc 9781119685401 epub3 035 r1.xhtml?
results.answer:

The retrieved evidence includes this book's table of contents but not the text of file 035 [S7]. results.question: What does the book say about miscellaneous drawing tips?
results.answer:
The book's scattered tips all circle one principle: a drawing must be readable at a glance, and everything else — bold marks, simplified design, dynamic poses — serves that goal.

## Marks, materials, and readability

Draw **BOLD**: grease pencil, marker, or 2B pencil, never a hard pencil, so drawings read from across the room — and number your drawings [S2]. Test clarity by blackening in the drawing: if you can still read what's happening, it works; keep decoration inside the main outline and make the outline itself interesting [S1][S22]. Drybrush (speed lines) and motion blur illustrate the optical blur of objects moving too fast to see, but use drybrush sparingly — only when drawings are so widely spaced the eye strains to connect them, since well-anticipated action lets the eye bridge big gaps on its own [S4][S21]. The book even notes, in its chiaroscuro chapter, that the line itself "never existed anyway" — it's a convention [S13][S23].

## Design, composition, and character

Draw for clarity, **one idea per sketch**, and put the important idea in the spotlight while everything else is subordinated to it [S3][S6][S7]. Avoid symmetry — it's boring and makes figures look cut out — so use angles, dynamic asymmetry, and straight lines played against curves for interest [S3][S6]. Draw borders so you compose to them, watch body landmarks like hipbones and ribs, and don't get too clever with camera angles, which often just make the drawing ambiguous [S6]. People are always "doing" something: express the purpose, feel the pose kinetically in your own body, show how the character feels, use straight-line symbols for stretches and bent lines for squashes, and darken pupils when drawing eyes [S3][S6].

## Observation, technique, and practice

Drawing takes two halves: technique knowledge (perspective, anatomy, force, shape) plus honest observation — when they combine, you can draw [S5][S19]. Diagnose your own work: generic? Look more. Specific but flat, dead, or poorly designed? Apply technique [S5]. Always start with a rough sketch that clarifies the image and the state of what you'll draw [S9]; don't be afraid to redraw, cut out parts that don't work, and have something to say rather than doodling [S3]. Drawing multiple moments of the same subject tells more than a single drawing and builds a sense of personality, proportion, and volume [S10][S25].

## Relevance to cinema

The tips are geared toward the screen and storyboard. Readability from across the room means a frame must register when projected; numbering keeps panels in sequence; composing to drawn borders anticipates the frame; and speed lines transfer fast motion into a static panel [S2][S4][S21]. Anticipation and overshoot studies map movement timing frame-by-frame, and finished boards get pitched to the production — the presentation step that follows storyboarding [S27][S17]. Shot design extends it further: camera placement, framing, and transitions are chosen to steer the viewer's eye across panels, so a storyboard remains legible as a sequence, not just as individual drawings [S30].

results.question: What does the book say about transcoding versus color rerendering?
results.answer:
The book draws a clean line between the two: **transcoding is a numerical color-space conversion, valid when displays differ only in their primaries; color rerendering is a perceptual transform, required when displays or their viewing environments differ substantially** [S1][S2].

**When transcoding works** — if two displays match in black levels, white luminance, gamma, and viewing conditions, and differ only in primary chromaticities, you can transcode: linearize the first display's encoded RGB values, convert them to CIE XYZ, convert those XYZ values to the second display's RGB, then reimpose the encoding nonlinearity [S2]. No appearance decisions are involved; it's a pure arithmetic remap through CIE XYZ.

**When color rerendering is needed** — if contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions are grossly dissimilar, the best solution is color rerendering: undo whatever color rendering was done for the first display, then color render the non-color-rendered CIE XYZ values for the second display [S1]. The book defines color rendering, in color science terms, as "the transformation of an image to account for differences in viewing environment" [S4] — the canonical example being a camera color-rendering a JPEG so desert sunlight reproduces acceptably on an office monitor [S4].

| Aspect | Transcoding | Color rerendering |
|---|---|---|
| Valid when | Viewing conditions, gamma, and luminance match; primaries differ | Contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions grossly differ |
| Operation | Linearize → CIE XYZ → second RGB → re-encode [S2] | Undo first display's rendering → render XYZ for second display [S1] |
| Frame of reference | Colorimetric (numbers) | Perceptual (appearance) |

The workflow implication is that the choice is forced by how different the two end points really are, and that color rendering is easier to do than to undo — which is why raw camera encodings deliberately leave it for downstream, rather than baking it in like a non-raw format [S6]. The book's ACES material shows the same idea institutionalized: the RRT supplies the color appearance "rendering" for dark-surround theatrical viewing, and the ODT then adapts that rendered image per display device [S3][S9].

results.question: What does the book say about affect, fatigue, and injury are control states?
results.answer:
The book treats affect, fatigue, and injury as persistent hidden control states — not cosmetic readouts, but state that must persist across beats, change only through observable causes, and visibly alter how the body moves. Each one is defined less by its psychology and more by the control it exerts downstream, with dedicated verification metrics and explicit failure states.

| Control state | Definition | Control function | Failure signature |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Affect** | Continuous vector A(t) = [v, a, d], v,a,d ∈ [-1,1], varying smoothly across a shot [S1] | Drives expression and action; experienced vs displayed affect may diverge [S3][S7] | Emotion appears only in a label or face, with no visible/tactical consequence [S6] |
| **Fatigue** | Taxed regions alter later capacity, variability, timing, or tactic [S6] | Modulates subsequent motion quality and scope after effort events | Exertion never changes later action [S6] |
| **Injury** | Declared mechanical effects and compensations that persist [S6] | Constrains affected regions; compensation must remain visible | Injured region performs at baseline without cause [S6] |

The shared mechanism is the point: all three live in the state-and-transition layer of the generation pipeline (actor state, support state, contact state, continuity state) and feed control composition — its scope, lifetime, envelope, priority, conflict, and freedom budget [S15]. Verification checks that expected state facts are still respected later (state persistence recall) and that hard facts never change without an observed cause, with the uncaused state-change rate targeted at zero [S6]. The doctrine's failure modes enforce the same idea: `continuity_break` means hidden state changed without cause and must be repaired by preserving persistence, while `causal_confusion` means succession was mistaken for causation [S12].

Affect is specified in the dimensional tradition — Russell's valence–arousal circumplex and Mehrabian & Russell's added dominance dimension, operationalized via the Self-Assessment Manikin [S2][S5] — and the corpus is careful about its boundaries: valence does not uniquely determine expression, and dominance is not model guidance strength or an objective personality score [S4]. Its cinematic usefulness comes from smooth variation: a frightened but composed character combines negative valence, elevated arousal, and moderate-to-high control, whereas a panicked character pairs similar valence and arousal with low control [S1]. Experienced affect (the directorial construct) and displayed affect (what the character reveals) are tracked separately and may deliberately diverge [S4].

Fatigue and injury are specified operationally through their metrics rather than physiology: fatigue propagation expects taxed regions to change later capacity, variability, timing, or tactic, and injury compensation consistency expects declared mechanical effects and their compensations to persist, with critical injuries required to pass [S6]. What the corpus doesn't supply is a deeper generative model for either — the definitions come through the verification contract (inputs, formulas, tolerances) and the failure signatures that catch violations.

results.question: What does the book say about movement of an object with a background?
results.answer:
The book treats object movement and background as a single perceptual system: movement is only visible relative to the frame line, and the background is what lets the viewer read that movement correctly [S6][S9].

**Movement types involving background**

| Type | What happens | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Relative movement | An object is gauged by its changing position against a stationary second object or the frame (a black circle moving past a fixed green circle) | [S4][S22] |
| Induced movement | A moving object transfers its motion to a nearby stationary object, so the stationary one appears to move and the mover appears still | [S2] |
| Apparent movement | A camera pan makes background elements stream past, transferring their motion to a subject that is actually stationary in the frame (trees passing behind a car) | [S10] |

Visual movement exists in the screen world only when something moves in relation to the frame line; when nothing does, there's no movement [S9]. Camera movement transfers itself to the objects in front of the lens, which is why FG, MG, and BG objects show distinct speed differences during two- and three-dimensional camera moves [S12].

**Principles for combining a moving object with a background**

Three visual factors govern the composite: the direction of the track the moving object creates, the orientation or angle of the background's linear motif, and the contrast or affinity produced when the two combine [S11]. A stretch of forest example makes this concrete: the car circles the camera while the camera pans with it, so the car stays put relative to the frame but the background trees stream by in the opposite direction of the pan — the trees generate apparent movement that the viewer transfers to the car [S10].

On the practical side, the book covers several techniques. **Motion tracking** analyzes an object's motion into a path, and other clips or elements can be attached to that path (in Fusion, clips need a transform node to inherit tracked motion) [S20][S23]. **Match moving** handles moving-camera shots: when the foreground camera moves, the background must move correspondingly, so tracking data is extracted from the foreground image and applied to the background during compositing unless the plates were shot with a motion-control camera [S7][S19]. Tracking also works the other way — a planet background can be made to follow the camera movement of the foreground shot, a technique the book says recurs in color grading [S5]. For motion-blurred subjects, a blurred rotoshape extracts the object cleanly over a neutral background, but a detailed background defeats the matte because any soft-edged matte that captures the blur also captures background detail [S1].

**Cinematic examples**

- Two-house shot (Figure): one wide shot of an actor standing in a doorway, then a close-up, showing the continuum of movement across edits [S17]. Shot #1 shows movement from Q7 (lower left) to Q9 (lower right) in a straight line, and Shot #2's curved movement picks up where Shot #1 ended [S8].
- A telephoto lens' reduced field of view, combined with a circular tracking move around a static subject, makes the background appear to revolve quickly behind the subject — an unusual perception effect that pairs camera movement with lens optics [S16].

One underlying rule connects all of these: any object that moves in relation to the frame generates a *track*, and movement is categorized by direction, quality, scale, and speed [S6]. The background is not a passive backdrop; it is the reference system against which all object motion becomes readable, and the technique to keep it aligned with the foreground is tracking and match moving [S5][S7].

results.question: What does the book say about sound editing?
results.answer:
**Sound editing is the post-production process of creating, shaping, and mixing the film's entire soundtrack — the sound details are worked out in the editing phase, and anything the production didn't capture in original sound is created during postproduction [S1].**

## What it is and where it sits

Sound editing is more elaborate than picture editing because it involves far more tracks and many more decisions, and a wrong decision can readily undermine the visuals [S1]. That care in building and mixing tracks applies across the scale of production, from a simple music video with two tracks to a blockbuster action film with 62 or more [S6]. The final track is assembled from **dialogue, ambience, hard sound effects, and foley sounds**, and a well-populated, well-mixed sound track earns descriptions like "full," "rich," "engrossing," and "powerful" [S8][S9]. Editors and sound designers gather additional audio during postproduction that augments — and sometimes replaces — production sound, generating a new, even more realistic-feeling "reality" for the narrative [S9][S24].

The sound designer is the creative analog of the director of photography: once dialogue editing is finished, the creative process begins, and the designer is responsible for the audience's overall acoustic experience [S8][S18]. This is why professional productions spend so much time, talent, and money on soundtracks — high-quality sound is essential to visual storytelling [S27]. Even "silent" films were never meant to be silent; music was arranged to accompany screenings purely because of technological limits, since early sound recording made editing so difficult that a cut meant losing image and sound together until rerecording and multiple cameras became common [S7][S14].

## How the sound edit proceeds

The editor's first task is determining the narrative point of a scene and then surrounding it with sound — as in *The Battle of Algiers*, where authenticity is central to our involvement [S1]. The rough sound edit mirrors the rough picture assembly: its goal is believability of performance and a progressive sense of story, while dramatic emphasis and metaphor wait for the fine cut; the editor likewise decides how much or how little dialogue the scene needs [S12]. During the edit is the time to experiment with speed and pitch manipulation, and at the end the sound editor creates an overall design that is transmitted to the director as a guide for rerecording [S2][S4]. Timecode from the original sources helps maintain sync between picture and sound tracks in the edited sequence [S15].

Foley work builds effects from everyday materials — cheese grating for a laser-saber hum, cellophane for fire, salt sprinkled on paper for rain, rice for hail, hands on soggy newspaper for footsteps in mud — while filters such as pitch shifting, time compression, reverb, equalization, and hum removal handle trickier signal problems [S31][S32]. Mixing typically happens in software integrated with the edit itself, such as DaVinci Resolve's Fairlight page, which lets editors refine edit, effects, color, and sound mix right up until mastering [S10][S30].

## Core principles

**Believability is the most urgent goal of the sound edit.** Because sound is processed more rapidly than visuals, an unbelievable track undermines the picture and loses audience involvement, making narrative clarity and believability the primary goals of the first phase of the edit [S11]. Sound also works on audiences on physiological, psychological, and emotional levels, which is why techniques like sound bridges (sound leading picture) smooth continuity and guide the viewer [S7][S16][S31]. Creatively, sound can be treated as raw material — musique concrète-style incorporation of any kind of sound, pattern-hunting on a sound map, and foley fictions that build a "reality" stronger than what was recorded on set [S29][S32].

results.question: What does the book say about write radio sparely?
results.answer:
The book's core rule for radio is to underwrite: "Overwriting is the most common mistake people make in radio. Be a genius. Underwrite" [S3]. Sparse writing means giving the script as few words as the idea allows, with one caveat — spare is the default "unless your concept demands a lot of words and fast action" [S2][S16]. It even offers a calibration: if a 60-second spot is a house, a :30 is a tent, and a :30 runs to roughly 60 words [S21].

The techniques it prescribes for keeping scripts spare:

- **Time the mandatories first.** Write legal disclaimers and required tags as sparely as possible, time them, and build the actual commercial into whatever time remains [S1][S3].
- **Write for a slow read.** Trim words so the voice talent can read slowly, quietly, one word at a time [S2].
- **Scribble concepts, not scripts.** Generate many ideas first, jotting each general concept on a Post-it note before writing anything out [S5].
- **Attack the brief one spot at a time.** If one spot develops a repeatable format, turn it into a campaign; otherwise write the funniest, coolest, or scariest spots you can — written to one strategy, they add up to one brand either way [S8].
- **Leave silence in the script.** Bare-bones execution "leaps out of the radio," and silence is to radio what white space is to print — it enlarges the idea it surrounds [S10].

The reason is twofold. Practically, it keeps you out of the studio-editing trap: showing up with a fat script means editing under pressure and without client approval, and promotional tags clients tack on the end eat into the total time [S1][S4]. Creatively, restraint is itself the strategy, since silence makes the idea feel bigger [S10].

The corpus shows the style in action. One example pairs sparse lines with surprise: "Two unexpected ideas. Both create surprise. Radios are pieces of furniture, not something to slip into a pocket. Men don't walk on the moon. It's a long way up. The air is thin" [S9]. Another: "A more responsive form of foreign aid would be to send them beer. American-made Red, White and Blue beer. Red, White and Blue is less expensive than planes or computers" [S17]. That surprise mechanism is the same one behind the Sony pocket-radio story — radios were pieces of furniture, not pocket items, so the idea was preposterous enough to seize attention [S12][S13]. Two practical facts round this out: radio spots typically run 10 to 60 seconds, with long-form "brokered time" up to an hour, and a spot only pays off with frequency — it must be repeated often to be effective [S11][S14].
